# 🧱 mBlock beginner examples: IMU Gyro

[🔙 Back to the IMU Gyro product page](/en/sensors/imu/index.md)

This page is for people who have **never written a program**: read the IMU Gyro on an **mBot** with mBlock 5 blocks. The 5 examples start with "turn the number into a sound" and work up to a robot that drives itself. Every example has a block picture, a downloadable project file and an Arduino sketch that does the same thing.

| Software | Who it suits | How to open the example file |
|---|---|---|
| 🟧 **mBlock 5 desktop** (blocks, Upload mode) + **MBC Pro Sensors extension v2** | Schools, first time with an mBot | Download the `.mblock` → open mBlock 5 → "File → Open from your computer" → switch to "Upload" at the bottom right → "Upload" |
| 🔧 **Arduino IDE** (text code) | People who want to see what is behind the blocks, or write their own code | Download the `.ino` → install the Makeblock and MBC_Sensors libraries (see [Makeblock extension](/en/makeblock.md)) → board Arduino Uno → upload |

> [!IMPORTANT]
> - The sensor must be the **Makeblock edition with the 2026-10 protocol v2 firmware**, connected through the **mBot socket board** to an RJ25 port; use extension **v2.0.0** (old firmware goes with the old v1 extension; they cannot be mixed).
> - The board is the **mBot (mCore)**. mBot Ranger, Orion and MegaPi work too: swap "when mBot starts up" for that board's hat block and use a port that board allows (see [supported boards and ports](/en/makeblock.md)); the mBot2 (CyberPi) has no RJ25 port and is not supported.
> - mBlock 5 is shown here with its English block text; your copy may show the same blocks in another language.

## Before you start

<figure class="ref-fig"><img src="/images/figures/imu/wiring-mbot.svg" alt="IMU Gyro × mBot wiring" loading="lazy"></figure>

Sensor → mBot socket board → RJ25 port on the board (S1 = host TX, S2 = host RX, UART 38400).

1. **Install the extension**: get the **MBC Pro Sensors v2.0.0** `.mext` from [Makeblock extension](/en/makeblock.md) and drop it into the mBlock 5 window; add **mBot** under "Devices" (bottom left) and switch to "Upload" (bottom right).
2. **Wiring**: IMU gyro → mBot socket board → mBot **port 2** (every example on this page uses this port; to use another, change the port number on the blocks).
3. **Let it boot first**: every example starts with "wait 1 seconds" so the sensor can boot; reading too early gives -32768 (nothing received yet).
4. Mount the IMU flat and firmly on the robot with **the board's printed X axis along the forward direction**; keep the robot still at power-on and when "zero heading" runs. Seen from above, **turning right makes the heading grow** (90° right = 90); it accumulates and never wraps back to 0.

## Blocks used on this page

Each reporter block is one "value id" of the sensor's value table (the same ids as the Arduino I2C registers); the full block list is in [Makeblock extension](/en/makeblock.md).

| Block | Returns | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| IMU Gyro port [2] pitch angle | -90~+90 ° | elevation of the board's printed X axis above horizontal: +90 pointing up, −90 pointing down, 0 level (from the gravity vector) |
| IMU Gyro port [2] gyro 1D heading | -32768~32767 ° | heading integrated about the yaw axis only, degrees, 0 at boot/zero; may exceed 360 |
| IMU Gyro port [2] zero heading | — | zero all four headings (zeroHeadings()); EV3 also accepts the stock gyro-reset WRITE 0x11 |

**Examples on this page**

1. [Tilt changes the pitch](#example-1-tilt-changes-the-pitch)
2. [The LED shows the heading](#example-2-the-led-shows-the-heading)
3. [Tilt drives one wheel](#example-3-tilt-drives-one-wheel)
4. [Drive straight with correction](#example-4-drive-straight-with-correction)
5. [Drive, turn 90°, drive again](#example-5-drive-turn-90%C2%B0-drive-again)

> [!NOTE]
> The `.mblock` files are generated in the mBlock 5 save format and **have not yet been opened in mBlock 5 for verification** (pending the extension v2 release). If one will not open or shows blank blocks, check that extension v2 is loaded and the device is mBot, or rebuild it from the block picture below (under 5 minutes); you can also [tell us on LINE](https://line.me/R/ti/p/@692vcvuk).

## Example 1: Tilt changes the pitch

**What this example does**: The mBot has no screen, so this example turns the "pitch angle" (nose up or down in degrees, 0 when flat) into a buzzer pitch: 440 Hz flat, higher nose-up, lower nose-down. Learn to "read the number" first.

**What you need**
- mBot (mCore board) + mBlock 5 desktop
- IMU Gyro (Makeblock edition) + mBot socket board

**Wiring**: IMU gyro → mBot socket board → mBot **port 2**. Mount it flat and firmly on the robot with the board's printed X axis along the robot's forward direction. Keep the robot still when the program starts.

**Download**

| mBlock 5 project | Equivalent Arduino sketch |
|---|---|
| [ex01_tilt_tone.mblock](/examples/imu/mblock/ex01_tilt_tone.mblock) | [ex01_tilt_tone.ino](/examples/imu/mblock/ex01_tilt_tone/ex01_tilt_tone.ino) |

<details open>
<summary>🧱 mBlock blocks (just rebuild them like this)</summary>

<pre class="blocks">when mBot starts up :: events hat
wait (1) seconds
forever
  play tone ((440) + ((IMU Gyro port [2 v] pitch angle :: #D9480F) * (4))) Hz for (0.1) seconds :: sound
end</pre>

</details>

<details>
<summary>🔧 Equivalent Arduino sketch (mBot)</summary>

```cpp
// IMU Gyro × mBlock 5  Example 1: Tilt changes the pitch  (equivalent Arduino sketch for mBot)
// Wiring: IMU gyro → mBot socket board → mBot port 2. Mount it flat and firmly on the robot with the board's printed X axis along the robot's forward direction. Keep the robot still when the program starts.
// Does exactly what the mBlock block example does, for people who want to see "what is behind the blocks" or use the Arduino IDE.
// Libraries needed:
//   1. Makeblock (Arduino IDE Library Manager, search "Makeblock", or the copy inside the mBlock 5 install folder)
//   2. MBC_Sensors v2: the four files in src/ of the extension .mext (MBC_Sensors.h/.cpp, mbc_proto.h, mbc_ids.h),
//      put them in Documents/Arduino/libraries/MBC_Sensors/ and #include <MBC_Sensors.h> (https://mbc-pro-sensors.github.io/en/makeblock.html)
// Board: Arduino Uno (the mBot mCore is an Uno). After uploading, unplug USB and run on battery.

#include <MeMCore.h>            // mBot (mCore): motors, LED, buzzer
#include <SoftwareSerial.h>
#include <MBC_Sensors.h>        // MBC sensors v2 (the same library the mBlock extension uses)

MBCPort mbc_port2(2);           // sensor on mBot port 2
MeDCMotor motorL(9);           // left wheel (M1)
MeDCMotor motorR(10);          // right wheel (M2)
MeRGBLed rgbled(7, 2);         // on-board RGB LED (2 pixels)
MeBuzzer buzzer;               // on-board buzzer

// left / right wheel power -100~100 (positive = forward): the mBot left wheel is mounted mirrored, so M1 gets the negative value; % becomes PWM 0~255
void wheels(int l, int r) {
  l = constrain(l, -100, 100); r = constrain(r, -100, 100);
  motorL.run(-l * 255 / 100);
  motorR.run(r * 255 / 100);
}

void setup() {   // everything runs inside setup(), just like the program mBlock generates
  mbc_port2.begin();
  delay(1000);   // Wait 1 s for the sensor to boot
  while (1) {   // Repeat forever
    buzzer.tone((440 + (mbcRead(mbc_port2, 0x06) * 4)), 100);   // Pitch = 440 + pitch angle × 4 Hz, for 0.1 s
  }
}

void loop() {}   // nothing here: the blocks above never return
```

</details>

**Step by step**
1. Wait 1 s for the sensor to boot
2. Repeat forever
   - Pitch = 440 + pitch angle × 4 Hz, for 0.1 s

**What you should see**: Robot flat: 440 Hz. Raise the nose slowly and the pitch rises (about 620 Hz at 45°); lower the nose and it drops.

**FAQ**
- **No sound?** → The buzzer is on the board and is not loud; listen closely, or change 0.1 s to 0.3 s.
- **Nose up gives a lower note?** → Normal: the sign depends on mounting. Mount the sensor rotated 180°, or change × 4 to × -4.
- **The robot is still but the heading slowly drifts?** → The robot must be completely still at power-on or zeroing. Put it down, unplug the sensor and plug it back in, then try again.
- **Nothing happens, or the value stays at -32768?** → Wrong port (every example on this page uses port 2), socket board not seated, or the sensor is not the Makeblock edition. Check with the "MBC common → connected?" block first; "protocol version" must read 2 for the new firmware (old firmware needs extension v1).
- **Upload fails, or the blocks are blank?** → Make sure the switch at the bottom right is in "Upload" mode, extension v2 has been dropped into mBlock, and the USB cable goes to the mBot board.

## Example 2: The LED shows the heading

**What this example does**: Zero the heading at the start, then turn the robot by hand: more than 20° to the right → blue, more than 20° to the left → red, facing the original direction → green. The decision skeleton for "drive straight" and "turn 90°" later.

**What you need**
- mBot (mCore board) + mBlock 5 desktop
- IMU Gyro (Makeblock edition) + mBot socket board

**Wiring**: IMU gyro → mBot socket board → mBot **port 2**. Mount it flat and firmly on the robot with the board's printed X axis along the robot's forward direction. Keep the robot still when the program starts.

**Download**

| mBlock 5 project | Equivalent Arduino sketch |
|---|---|
| [ex02_led_heading.mblock](/examples/imu/mblock/ex02_led_heading.mblock) | [ex02_led_heading.ino](/examples/imu/mblock/ex02_led_heading/ex02_led_heading.ino) |

<details open>
<summary>🧱 mBlock blocks (just rebuild them like this)</summary>

<pre class="blocks">when mBot starts up :: events hat
wait (1) seconds
IMU Gyro port [2 v] zero heading :: #D9480F
forever
  if &lt;(IMU Gyro port [2 v] gyro 1D heading :: #D9480F) &gt; (20)&gt; then
    LED [all v] colour red (0) green (0) blue (255) :: looks
  else
    if &lt;(IMU Gyro port [2 v] gyro 1D heading :: #D9480F) &lt; (-20)&gt; then
      LED [all v] colour red (255) green (0) blue (0) :: looks
    else
      LED [all v] colour red (0) green (255) blue (0) :: looks
    end
  end
end</pre>

</details>

<details>
<summary>🔧 Equivalent Arduino sketch (mBot)</summary>

```cpp
// IMU Gyro × mBlock 5  Example 2: The LED shows the heading  (equivalent Arduino sketch for mBot)
// Wiring: IMU gyro → mBot socket board → mBot port 2. Mount it flat and firmly on the robot with the board's printed X axis along the robot's forward direction. Keep the robot still when the program starts.
// Does exactly what the mBlock block example does, for people who want to see "what is behind the blocks" or use the Arduino IDE.
// Libraries needed:
//   1. Makeblock (Arduino IDE Library Manager, search "Makeblock", or the copy inside the mBlock 5 install folder)
//   2. MBC_Sensors v2: the four files in src/ of the extension .mext (MBC_Sensors.h/.cpp, mbc_proto.h, mbc_ids.h),
//      put them in Documents/Arduino/libraries/MBC_Sensors/ and #include <MBC_Sensors.h> (https://mbc-pro-sensors.github.io/en/makeblock.html)
// Board: Arduino Uno (the mBot mCore is an Uno). After uploading, unplug USB and run on battery.

#include <MeMCore.h>            // mBot (mCore): motors, LED, buzzer
#include <SoftwareSerial.h>
#include <MBC_Sensors.h>        // MBC sensors v2 (the same library the mBlock extension uses)

MBCPort mbc_port2(2);           // sensor on mBot port 2
MeDCMotor motorL(9);           // left wheel (M1)
MeDCMotor motorR(10);          // right wheel (M2)
MeRGBLed rgbled(7, 2);         // on-board RGB LED (2 pixels)
MeBuzzer buzzer;               // on-board buzzer

// left / right wheel power -100~100 (positive = forward): the mBot left wheel is mounted mirrored, so M1 gets the negative value; % becomes PWM 0~255
void wheels(int l, int r) {
  l = constrain(l, -100, 100); r = constrain(r, -100, 100);
  motorL.run(-l * 255 / 100);
  motorR.run(r * 255 / 100);
}

void setup() {   // everything runs inside setup(), just like the program mBlock generates
  mbc_port2.begin();
  delay(1000);   // Wait 1 s for the sensor to boot
  mbcWrite(mbc_port2, 0xE0);   // Zero the heading: the current direction becomes 0
  while (1) {   // Repeat forever
    if ((mbcRead(mbc_port2, 0x03) > 20)) {   // If the gyro 1D heading is greater than 20
      rgbled.setColor(0, 0, 0, 255); rgbled.show();   // Turned right more than 20°: blue
    } else {
      if ((mbcRead(mbc_port2, 0x03) < -20)) {   // Otherwise, if the gyro 1D heading is less than -20
        rgbled.setColor(0, 255, 0, 0); rgbled.show();   // Turned left more than 20°: red
      } else {
        rgbled.setColor(0, 0, 255, 0); rgbled.show();   // Facing the original direction: green
      }
    }
  }
}

void loop() {}   // nothing here: the blocks above never return
```

</details>

**Step by step**
1. Wait 1 s for the sensor to boot
2. Zero the heading: the current direction becomes 0
3. Repeat forever
   - If the gyro 1D heading is greater than 20
      - Turned right more than 20°: blue
      - otherwise:
         - Otherwise, if the gyro 1D heading is less than -20
            - Turned left more than 20°: red
            - otherwise:
               - Facing the original direction: green

**What you should see**: Green at the start; turn the robot right and past 20° it goes blue; back again green; left past 20° red. A full turn comes back as 360, not 0, so it stays blue.

**FAQ**
- **Turning right gives red?** → The sensor is mounted upside down. Flip it, or swap 20 and -20 in the program.
- **The robot is still but the heading slowly drifts?** → The robot must be completely still at power-on or zeroing. Put it down, unplug the sensor and plug it back in, then try again.
- **Nothing happens, or the value stays at -32768?** → Wrong port (every example on this page uses port 2), socket board not seated, or the sensor is not the Makeblock edition. Check with the "MBC common → connected?" block first; "protocol version" must read 2 for the new firmware (old firmware needs extension v1).
- **Upload fails, or the blocks are blank?** → Make sure the switch at the bottom right is in "Upload" mode, extension v2 has been dropped into mBlock, and the USB cable goes to the mBot board.

## Example 3: Tilt drives one wheel

**What this example does**: Use "pitch angle × 2" directly as the left wheel power: nose up → forward, nose down → reverse, flat → still; the more tilt, the faster. Prop the robot up to watch.

**What you need**
- mBot (mCore board) + mBlock 5 desktop
- mBot two-wheel robot (left wheel on M1, right wheel on M2, as shipped)
- IMU Gyro (Makeblock edition) + mBot socket board

**Wiring**: IMU gyro → mBot socket board → mBot **port 2**. Mount it flat and firmly on the robot with the board's printed X axis along the robot's forward direction. Keep the robot still when the program starts.

**Download**

| mBlock 5 project | Equivalent Arduino sketch |
|---|---|
| [ex03_tilt_one_wheel.mblock](/examples/imu/mblock/ex03_tilt_one_wheel.mblock) | [ex03_tilt_one_wheel.ino](/examples/imu/mblock/ex03_tilt_one_wheel/ex03_tilt_one_wheel.ino) |

<details open>
<summary>🧱 mBlock blocks (just rebuild them like this)</summary>

<pre class="blocks">when mBot starts up :: events hat
wait (1) seconds
forever
  left wheel power ((IMU Gyro port [2 v] pitch angle :: #D9480F) * (2)) %, right wheel power (0) % :: motion
end</pre>

</details>

<details>
<summary>🔧 Equivalent Arduino sketch (mBot)</summary>

```cpp
// IMU Gyro × mBlock 5  Example 3: Tilt drives one wheel  (equivalent Arduino sketch for mBot)
// Wiring: IMU gyro → mBot socket board → mBot port 2. Mount it flat and firmly on the robot with the board's printed X axis along the robot's forward direction. Keep the robot still when the program starts.
// Does exactly what the mBlock block example does, for people who want to see "what is behind the blocks" or use the Arduino IDE.
// Libraries needed:
//   1. Makeblock (Arduino IDE Library Manager, search "Makeblock", or the copy inside the mBlock 5 install folder)
//   2. MBC_Sensors v2: the four files in src/ of the extension .mext (MBC_Sensors.h/.cpp, mbc_proto.h, mbc_ids.h),
//      put them in Documents/Arduino/libraries/MBC_Sensors/ and #include <MBC_Sensors.h> (https://mbc-pro-sensors.github.io/en/makeblock.html)
// Board: Arduino Uno (the mBot mCore is an Uno). After uploading, unplug USB and run on battery.

#include <MeMCore.h>            // mBot (mCore): motors, LED, buzzer
#include <SoftwareSerial.h>
#include <MBC_Sensors.h>        // MBC sensors v2 (the same library the mBlock extension uses)

MBCPort mbc_port2(2);           // sensor on mBot port 2
MeDCMotor motorL(9);           // left wheel (M1)
MeDCMotor motorR(10);          // right wheel (M2)
MeRGBLed rgbled(7, 2);         // on-board RGB LED (2 pixels)
MeBuzzer buzzer;               // on-board buzzer

// left / right wheel power -100~100 (positive = forward): the mBot left wheel is mounted mirrored, so M1 gets the negative value; % becomes PWM 0~255
void wheels(int l, int r) {
  l = constrain(l, -100, 100); r = constrain(r, -100, 100);
  motorL.run(-l * 255 / 100);
  motorR.run(r * 255 / 100);
}

void setup() {   // everything runs inside setup(), just like the program mBlock generates
  mbc_port2.begin();
  delay(1000);   // Wait 1 s for the sensor to boot
  while (1) {   // Repeat forever
    wheels((mbcRead(mbc_port2, 0x06) * 2), 0);   // Left wheel power = pitch angle × 2, right wheel 0
  }
}

void loop() {}   // nothing here: the blocks above never return
```

</details>

**Step by step**
1. Wait 1 s for the sensor to boot
2. Repeat forever
   - Left wheel power = pitch angle × 2, right wheel 0

**What you should see**: Flat: the left wheel is still; nose up 30° → the wheel runs forward at power 60; nose down → reverse.

**FAQ**
- **The robot turns the wrong way and gets worse?** → Swap the "+" and "−" (or swap the left and right wheel powers). The mBot ships with the left wheel on M1 and the right on M2; check your own wiring.
- **The wheel creeps when flat?** → The pitch is not always exactly 0. Add "if the absolute value is below 3 then power 0".
- **The robot is still but the heading slowly drifts?** → The robot must be completely still at power-on or zeroing. Put it down, unplug the sensor and plug it back in, then try again.
- **Nothing happens, or the value stays at -32768?** → Wrong port (every example on this page uses port 2), socket board not seated, or the sensor is not the Makeblock edition. Check with the "MBC common → connected?" block first; "protocol version" must read 2 for the new firmware (old firmware needs extension v1).
- **Upload fails, or the blocks are blank?** → Make sure the switch at the bottom right is in "Upload" mode, extension v2 has been dropped into mBlock, and the USB cable goes to the mBot board.

## Example 4: Drive straight with correction

**What this example does**: Two wheels never run at exactly the same speed, so a robot drifts. Zero the heading, then use "heading × 2" as the correction: drifting right (heading grows) → left wheel slower, right wheel faster, pulling the nose back.

**What you need**
- mBot (mCore board) + mBlock 5 desktop
- mBot two-wheel robot (left wheel on M1, right wheel on M2, as shipped)
- IMU Gyro (Makeblock edition) + mBot socket board

**Wiring**: IMU gyro → mBot socket board → mBot **port 2**. Mount it flat and firmly on the robot with the board's printed X axis along the robot's forward direction. Keep the robot still when the program starts.

**Download**

| mBlock 5 project | Equivalent Arduino sketch |
|---|---|
| [ex04_drive_straight.mblock](/examples/imu/mblock/ex04_drive_straight.mblock) | [ex04_drive_straight.ino](/examples/imu/mblock/ex04_drive_straight/ex04_drive_straight.ino) |

<details open>
<summary>🧱 mBlock blocks (just rebuild them like this)</summary>

<pre class="blocks">when mBot starts up :: events hat
wait (1) seconds
IMU Gyro port [2 v] zero heading :: #D9480F
forever
  set [fix v] to ((IMU Gyro port [2 v] gyro 1D heading :: #D9480F) * (2))
  left wheel power ((40) - (fix)) %, right wheel power ((40) + (fix)) % :: motion
end</pre>

</details>

<details>
<summary>🔧 Equivalent Arduino sketch (mBot)</summary>

```cpp
// IMU Gyro × mBlock 5  Example 4: Drive straight with correction  (equivalent Arduino sketch for mBot)
// Wiring: IMU gyro → mBot socket board → mBot port 2. Mount it flat and firmly on the robot with the board's printed X axis along the robot's forward direction. Keep the robot still when the program starts.
// Does exactly what the mBlock block example does, for people who want to see "what is behind the blocks" or use the Arduino IDE.
// Libraries needed:
//   1. Makeblock (Arduino IDE Library Manager, search "Makeblock", or the copy inside the mBlock 5 install folder)
//   2. MBC_Sensors v2: the four files in src/ of the extension .mext (MBC_Sensors.h/.cpp, mbc_proto.h, mbc_ids.h),
//      put them in Documents/Arduino/libraries/MBC_Sensors/ and #include <MBC_Sensors.h> (https://mbc-pro-sensors.github.io/en/makeblock.html)
// Board: Arduino Uno (the mBot mCore is an Uno). After uploading, unplug USB and run on battery.

#include <MeMCore.h>            // mBot (mCore): motors, LED, buzzer
#include <SoftwareSerial.h>
#include <MBC_Sensors.h>        // MBC sensors v2 (the same library the mBlock extension uses)

MBCPort mbc_port2(2);           // sensor on mBot port 2
MeDCMotor motorL(9);           // left wheel (M1)
MeDCMotor motorR(10);          // right wheel (M2)
MeRGBLed rgbled(7, 2);         // on-board RGB LED (2 pixels)
MeBuzzer buzzer;               // on-board buzzer
float fix = 0;                // variable：fix

// left / right wheel power -100~100 (positive = forward): the mBot left wheel is mounted mirrored, so M1 gets the negative value; % becomes PWM 0~255
void wheels(int l, int r) {
  l = constrain(l, -100, 100); r = constrain(r, -100, 100);
  motorL.run(-l * 255 / 100);
  motorR.run(r * 255 / 100);
}

void setup() {   // everything runs inside setup(), just like the program mBlock generates
  mbc_port2.begin();
  delay(1000);   // Wait 1 s for the sensor to boot
  mbcWrite(mbc_port2, 0xE0);   // Zero the heading: the current direction becomes 0
  while (1) {   // Repeat forever
    fix = (mbcRead(mbc_port2, 0x03) * 2);   // fix = gyro 1D heading × 2
    wheels((40 - fix), (40 + fix));   // Left = 40 − fix, right = 40 + fix: drifting right (positive heading) → left wheel slow, right wheel fast
  }
}

void loop() {}   // nothing here: the blocks above never return
```

</details>

**Step by step**
1. Wait 1 s for the sensor to boot
2. Zero the heading: the current direction becomes 0
3. Repeat forever
   - fix = gyro 1D heading × 2
   - Left = 40 − fix, right = 40 + fix: drifting right (positive heading) → left wheel slow, right wheel fast

**What you should see**: The robot drives straight; push the nose off course by hand and it turns back to the original direction and carries on.

**FAQ**
- **It drifts more and more, even spins?** → The correction is reversed (sensor mounted upside down): swap "40 − fix" and "40 + fix".
- **It shakes left and right?** → Lower × 2 (e.g. × 1).
- **The robot is still but the heading slowly drifts?** → The robot must be completely still at power-on or zeroing. Put it down, unplug the sensor and plug it back in, then try again.
- **Nothing happens, or the value stays at -32768?** → Wrong port (every example on this page uses port 2), socket board not seated, or the sensor is not the Makeblock edition. Check with the "MBC common → connected?" block first; "protocol version" must read 2 for the new firmware (old firmware needs extension v1).
- **Upload fails, or the blocks are blank?** → Make sure the switch at the bottom right is in "Upload" mode, extension v2 has been dropped into mBlock, and the USB cable goes to the mBot board.

## Example 5: Drive, turn 90°, drive again

**What this example does**: A classic competition move: drive 2 s → spin right until the heading reaches 90° → beep → drive 2 s more. Turning by gyro is far more accurate than "turn for N seconds": "wait until heading > 88" waits for the turn (2° left for braking). No "forever" here; it stops when done.

**What you need**
- mBot (mCore board) + mBlock 5 desktop
- mBot two-wheel robot (left wheel on M1, right wheel on M2, as shipped)
- IMU Gyro (Makeblock edition) + mBot socket board

**Wiring**: IMU gyro → mBot socket board → mBot **port 2**. Mount it flat and firmly on the robot with the board's printed X axis along the robot's forward direction. Keep the robot still when the program starts.

**Download**

| mBlock 5 project | Equivalent Arduino sketch |
|---|---|
| [ex05_turn_90.mblock](/examples/imu/mblock/ex05_turn_90.mblock) | [ex05_turn_90.ino](/examples/imu/mblock/ex05_turn_90/ex05_turn_90.ino) |

<details open>
<summary>🧱 mBlock blocks (just rebuild them like this)</summary>

<pre class="blocks">when mBot starts up :: events hat
wait (1) seconds
IMU Gyro port [2 v] zero heading :: #D9480F
left wheel power (40) %, right wheel power (40) % :: motion
wait (2) seconds
stop moving :: motion
wait (0.5) seconds
IMU Gyro port [2 v] zero heading :: #D9480F
left wheel power (25) %, right wheel power (-25) % :: motion
wait until &lt;(IMU Gyro port [2 v] gyro 1D heading :: #D9480F) &gt; (88)&gt;
stop moving :: motion
play tone (880) Hz for (0.3) seconds :: sound
left wheel power (40) %, right wheel power (40) % :: motion
wait (2) seconds
stop moving :: motion</pre>

</details>

<details>
<summary>🔧 Equivalent Arduino sketch (mBot)</summary>

```cpp
// IMU Gyro × mBlock 5  Example 5: Drive, turn 90°, drive again  (equivalent Arduino sketch for mBot)
// Wiring: IMU gyro → mBot socket board → mBot port 2. Mount it flat and firmly on the robot with the board's printed X axis along the robot's forward direction. Keep the robot still when the program starts.
// Does exactly what the mBlock block example does, for people who want to see "what is behind the blocks" or use the Arduino IDE.
// Libraries needed:
//   1. Makeblock (Arduino IDE Library Manager, search "Makeblock", or the copy inside the mBlock 5 install folder)
//   2. MBC_Sensors v2: the four files in src/ of the extension .mext (MBC_Sensors.h/.cpp, mbc_proto.h, mbc_ids.h),
//      put them in Documents/Arduino/libraries/MBC_Sensors/ and #include <MBC_Sensors.h> (https://mbc-pro-sensors.github.io/en/makeblock.html)
// Board: Arduino Uno (the mBot mCore is an Uno). After uploading, unplug USB and run on battery.

#include <MeMCore.h>            // mBot (mCore): motors, LED, buzzer
#include <SoftwareSerial.h>
#include <MBC_Sensors.h>        // MBC sensors v2 (the same library the mBlock extension uses)

MBCPort mbc_port2(2);           // sensor on mBot port 2
MeDCMotor motorL(9);           // left wheel (M1)
MeDCMotor motorR(10);          // right wheel (M2)
MeRGBLed rgbled(7, 2);         // on-board RGB LED (2 pixels)
MeBuzzer buzzer;               // on-board buzzer

// left / right wheel power -100~100 (positive = forward): the mBot left wheel is mounted mirrored, so M1 gets the negative value; % becomes PWM 0~255
void wheels(int l, int r) {
  l = constrain(l, -100, 100); r = constrain(r, -100, 100);
  motorL.run(-l * 255 / 100);
  motorR.run(r * 255 / 100);
}

void setup() {   // everything runs inside setup(), just like the program mBlock generates
  mbc_port2.begin();
  delay(1000);   // Wait 1 s for the sensor to boot
  mbcWrite(mbc_port2, 0xE0);   // Zero the heading: the current direction becomes 0
  wheels(40, 40);   // Drive straight
  delay(2000);   // For 2 s
  wheels(0, 0);   // Stop
  delay(500);   // Wait 0.5 s for the robot to settle
  mbcWrite(mbc_port2, 0xE0);   // Zero the heading: the current direction becomes 0
  wheels(25, -25);   // Left wheel forward, right wheel back: spin right (slower is more accurate)
  while (!(mbcRead(mbc_port2, 0x03) > 88)) delay(5);   // Wait until the heading is greater than 88°
  wheels(0, 0);   // At 90°: stop
  buzzer.tone(880, 300);   // Beep
  wheels(40, 40);   // Drive straight again
  delay(2000);   // For 2 s
  wheels(0, 0);   // Stop
}

void loop() {}   // nothing here: the blocks above never return
```

</details>

**Step by step**
1. Wait 1 s for the sensor to boot
2. Zero the heading: the current direction becomes 0
3. Drive straight
4. For 2 s
5. Stop
6. Wait 0.5 s for the robot to settle
7. Zero the heading: the current direction becomes 0
8. Left wheel forward, right wheel back: spin right (slower is more accurate)
9. Wait until the heading is greater than 88°
10. At 90°: stop
11. Beep
12. Drive straight again
13. For 2 s
14. Stop

**What you should see**: The robot drives 2 s, spins right about 90°, beeps, drives 2 s more and stops: an L shape.

**FAQ**
- **It always overshoots by a few degrees?** → Change 88 to 85, or lower the spin power 25.
- **It spins forever?** → The heading does not grow when turning right (sensor upside down): change "25, -25" to "-25, 25".
- **The robot is still but the heading slowly drifts?** → The robot must be completely still at power-on or zeroing. Put it down, unplug the sensor and plug it back in, then try again.
- **Nothing happens, or the value stays at -32768?** → Wrong port (every example on this page uses port 2), socket board not seated, or the sensor is not the Makeblock edition. Check with the "MBC common → connected?" block first; "protocol version" must read 2 for the new firmware (old firmware needs extension v1).
- **Upload fails, or the blocks are blank?** → Make sure the switch at the bottom right is in "Upload" mode, extension v2 has been dropped into mBlock, and the USB cable goes to the mBot board.
